newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore treasury profits up 21 pct in 1995.
newsitem.headline: Singapore treasury profits up 21 pct in 1995.

text.p: Treasury profits in Singapore rose 21 percent to Singapore $1.39 billion in 1995, the Singapore Foreign Exchange Market Committee (SFEMC) said in its annual report on Thursday.

Citing the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS)'s survey of treasury activities in 1995, the SFEMC said total revenue from foreign exchange operations alone rose 43 percent to S$792 million in 1995, but this was still below the average of S $870 million recorded from 1990 to 1994.
The SFEMC attributed the lower revenue to a reduced tolerance for risk among banks after the poor performance of 1994 and narrower margins due to increased competition and changes in technology.

Total direct costs rose 12 percent in 1995, in line with the previous year's increase. Expenditure on fixed assets rose 29 percent while technology costs were up 77 percent as a number of banks expanded, upgraded or relocated their dealing rooms.
Wages also posted an increase with average dealer remuneration rising 39 percent while wages for support staff rose 23 percent.
"The labour market was noticeably tight in the more technical and expertise-intensive areas of emerging markets and derivatives," the report said.
It said treasury managers needed to recognise the pitfalls of over-rapid expansion and to develop a long-term plan for their operations in Singapore.

In a survey of regional currencies and debt markets among Asian banks and investment houses, the SFEMC said Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia had active spot markets with daily trading volumes ranging from US$3.5 billion to US$6.0 billion.
Swap and forward volumes were estimated to be the highest in Thailand with US$9.0 billion traded daily.

The report said Asia's bond markets were relatively small and at an early stage of development, but added that private sector demand was expected to propel the Asian bond market to an estimated US$686 billion in 1996, from US$453 billion at the end of 1994.
